## Project Vision and Goals

I wanted a fast, private, desktop search tool for my personal notes — something
that could scan a folder full of `.txt` and `.md` files and surface results by
relevance without sending anything to the internet. No Electron, no web server,
no cloud. Just a compiled C++ binary that owns its own data.

The core of the project is an **inverted index** — the same fundamental data
structure that powers large-scale search engines. The idea is simple: instead of
searching through every file every time a query comes in, you build a map upfront
that goes from words to the files they appear in. Lookups then become direct
index hits rather than full scans.

The goals for this first phase were:

- Build an inverted index from a directory of text files
- Support exact and partial (substring) word matching
- Implement multi-word AND search with frequency-based scoring
- Extract a snippet showing where the term appears in the file
- Keep the architecture clean and extensible for future file types

## The Inverted Index

The index structure is defined in `Indexer.h`:

```cpp
using Index = std::unordered_map<std::string, std::unordered_map<std::string, int>>;
```

The outer map keys on a word. The inner map keys on a file path and stores the
frequency count of that word in that file. So after indexing a directory, a
lookup for `"algorithm"` might return:

```
"algorithm" -> {
    "notes/lecture1.txt": 4,
    "notes/dsa_review.md": 11,
    "notes/project.txt": 2
}
```

Frequency matters because it drives the relevance score — a file where your
search term appears 11 times is more relevant than one where it appears twice.

## Building the Index

The `Indexer` class scans a directory, filters for `.txt` and `.md` files, reads
each one, and populates the index. The entry point is `buildIndex()`:

```cpp
void Indexer::buildIndex(const std::string& directoryPath) {
    index.clear();
    for (const auto& entry : fs::directory_iterator(directoryPath)) {
        std::string ext = entry.path().extension().string();
        if (ext == ".txt" || ext == ".md") {
            processFile(entry.path().string());
        }
    }
}
```

Each file is read into a string and passed to `tokenize()`, which strips
punctuation and converts everything to lowercase. The resulting words are then
inserted into the index with their file path and incremented frequency count:

```cpp
for (const auto& word : words) {
    index[word][filePath] += 1;
}
```

## Shared Tokenization

Both the `Indexer` and `SearchEngine` need to tokenize text — the indexer when
building, the engine when processing a query. Having two separate implementations
would risk inconsistency, so tokenization lives in a shared header `Tokenizer.h`
as an `inline` free function:

```cpp
inline std::vector<std::string> tokenize(const std::string& text) {
    std::vector<std::string> tokens;
    std::string current;

    for (char c : text) {
        unsigned char uc = static_cast<unsigned char>(c);
        if (std::isalnum(uc)) {
            current += static_cast<char>(std::tolower(uc));
        } else if (!current.empty()) {
            tokens.push_back(current);
            current.clear();
        }
    }
    if (!current.empty()) tokens.push_back(current);
    return tokens;
}
```

Using `inline` here is intentional — it tells the linker to expect this
definition in multiple translation units and merge them, avoiding duplicate
symbol errors without needing a separate `.cpp` file.

## Search and Scoring

The `SearchEngine` class takes a const reference to the completed index — no
copy, just a view into the data the `Indexer` already owns.

Queries are tokenized the same way as the index content, which guarantees that
`"Binary Tree"` and `"binary tree"` resolve to the same tokens and hit the same
index entries.

For each query term, `getFilesForTerm()` first checks for an exact match, then
falls back to substring matching across all index keys:

```cpp
// Exact match
auto it = index.find(term);

// Partial match fallback
for (const auto& kv : index) {
    if (kv.first.find(term) != std::string::npos) {
        // accumulate scores
    }
}
```

This means searching `"tree"` will also surface files containing `"trees"` or
`"subtree"` — useful when you don't remember the exact form of a word.

Multi-word queries apply AND logic: a file must contain matches for every term
to appear in results. The total score is the sum of frequencies across all
matched terms, and results are sorted highest score first with alphabetical
tie-breaking.

## Snippet Extraction

Results include a short preview showing where the term appears in the file.
`extractSnippet()` finds the first occurrence of the search word in the file
content and returns a 120-character window centered around it:

```cpp
int window = 60;
std::size_t start = (pos > static_cast<std::size_t>(window)) ? pos - window : 0;
std::size_t end = std::min(pos + lowerWord.length() + window, content.size());
std::string snippet = content.substr(start, end - start);
```

Newlines are replaced with spaces so the snippet renders cleanly on a single
line, wrapped in `...` ellipses.

## Reflection

The trickiest part was getting the AND search logic right with partial matching
in play. Because `getFilesForTerm()` returns files for both exact and substring
hits, a file can satisfy a term match via a substring even if the exact word
doesn't appear. That's by design, but it's worth understanding — searching
`"hash table"` could match a file containing `"hashtable"` and `"turntable"`
even if neither exact word appears independently.

The architecture decision I'm most satisfied with is keeping tokenization shared
and consistent. It's a small thing but eliminates an entire class of subtle bugs
where the indexer and search engine would process text differently.

## What's Next

The backend is complete and tested. The next phase is wrapping it in a proper
desktop GUI using Qt Widgets — a native Windows application with a directory
picker, search bar, and results list, all backed by the same pure C++ engine
built here.
